title: Biographical basics; family background
description: Stella Reif gives her maiden name Stone, birth in South Dakota around 1900, and current address in Clarkston. She explains that her family moved by train to Idaho around 1909 when she was about seven, settling in the Lewiston area where her father worked as a stonemason and contractor.

title: Father's stonework; mother's crafts; parents' details
description: Reif describes her father's work building houses and carving stone, including a lion head fountain in Lewiston. She also discusses her mother Smith's skills at sewing and knitting, and identifies her husband Fred Reif and their marriage details.

title: Children; family losses
description: She names her three sons Donald, Eldin, and Fred, noting the recent death of her eldest at 59, the loss of baby Fred at two weeks old, and Donald's residence in Santa Barbara. She also mentions her own sister who lives in California.

title: Education; photography career
description: Reif discusses her high school education, brief business college attendance, and her long career working in a Lewiston photography studio. She describes learning darkroom techniques, retouching, and printing from her employer.

title: Crafts; fair prizes; sewing
description: She describes her hobbies including flower-making, tatting, crochet, and embroidery, noting that she and her mother won many prizes at fairs. She also mentions teaching quilting and other crafts at the senior center.

title: Church choir; senior center work
description: Reif talks about singing in the church choir until their director passed away, her current part-time work at the senior center, driving the bus, and teaching flower-making classes.

title: School days; sports; motorcycle
description: She recalls starting school at age five, playing basketball and baseball, doing trapeze in the barn, and adventures riding a motorcycle with a sidecar. She also mentions a strict principal and her general enjoyment of school.

title: Marriage decision; farm life
description: Reif explains how she decided to work rather than go away to school, met her husband, and moved to farm life. She describes farming wheat, raising cattle and chickens, and cooking for threshing crews.

title: Caring for mother; family support
description: She describes caring for her elderly mother for ten years, her brother-in-law's gratitude for past kindnesses, and her philosophy about not burdening her children with her own care.

title: Depression; wartime
description: Reif recounts the hardships of the Depression, wheat prices at 22 cents, selling horses, and returning to photography work. She also discusses her husband's rejection from World War II service due to flat feet.

title: Farm modernization; sausage making
description: She explains the decision not to buy expensive new machinery, reducing the farm to 42 acres, and their business butchering pigs and making sausage for sale.

title: Retirement; house improvements; later work
description: Reif describes her husband's retirement, her work as head housekeeper at a college, modernizing their Pullman-area home with plumbing and electricity, and their travels after retirement.

title: Courtship; meeting husband; marriage
description: She tells of meeting Fred Reif at a dance, double dating with her sister, their courtship of almost a year, their happy marriage, and business decisions they made together.

title: Childbirth and midwife care; family size; raising siblings
description: Stella Reif describes giving birth with a midwife for Donnie while her other sons were born in a hospital. She explains that she wanted four children but had three boys, and discusses raising her younger sister as a daughter after their father died. She also recalls a hired man with several children and how she sewed for them.

title: Caring for foster children
description: She recounts taking in a young girl with curly hair whose mother was sick a lot, sewing clothes for her, and taking her to the hospital because the child was very ill. She describes the emotional satisfaction of fostering, noting that one foster son in Oregon now has five children who treat her like a grandmother, and how deeply this young man valued their parental relationship.

title: Dairy farm work; cream money and chickens
description: She describes milking about ten cows by hand and how the cream money provided their grocery funds and extras like dancing. She mentions they sold butter instead of raw cream and kept chickens mostly for meat rather than eggs.

title: Social clubs; political attitudes; church involvement
description: She identifies herself as a member of the Rebecca Lodge and other social clubs but explains she did not belong to political organizations. She describes herself as independent in voting rather than strictly Republican, while her husband was a good Republican. She discusses her strong involvement in church work teaching Sunday school for many years.

title: Memories; widowhood; maintaining the farm
description: She reflects on her happiest and hardest memories, stating that losing her husband was the hardest thing she faced. She explains how she tried to keep up their large property, including his half-acre of iris and garden, but eventually hired Ed Bell to help. She describes getting up very early until late at night working on the property before deciding to sell the house and eight acres.

title: Current home; gardening; hobbies; health
description: She describes moving into a two-bedroom house where she lives alone and continues gardening because she considers herself still a farmer. She discusses knitting Afghans and making quilt samples in the evenings, noting she reads magazines but rarely books. She mentions that she has never been much of a reader since her mother discouraged reading to save electricity when she was young.

title: Health and activity; river swimming; laundry technology
description: She discusses maintaining good health through staying active and walking fast, recalling how she used to swim in the river at Clarkteton with other girls who worked until five o'clock. She then describes the old technology of washing clothes on a board and making her own soap, including the labor of hauling water and ironing with flat irons heated on a stove.
